text: [excited] This is Max. This morning, Max woke up able to read minds. [deadpan] His first ever mind-read was the dog. It said "food." Great start. [tense] Then he found this under his door. [whisper] "I can read minds too. I know what you're thinking. Midnight." [tense] Someone else has the power. Someone who knows him. And Max has until midnight to find out who. [pause] Luckily, he can read minds. Unluckily... so can they.

[excited] Suspect one. Zoe. She sits across from Max on the bus every single morning. Max focuses. And for the first time in his life, he hears what a girl actually thinks about him. [whisper] "...he's cute." [deadpan] Not exactly a criminal mastermind. Suspect one, cleared. [excited] Nine a.m. The maths exam. Max doesn't need to study. The teacher is literally thinking the answers. [sarcastic] One hundred percent. Again. The teacher is now thinking a word we can't put on YouTube. But it can't be him. His brain is too busy wondering where he left his car.

[curious] Lunch. Max tries to read a stranger. And gets... nothing. [curious] Here's why, and it's real. In 2023, scientists in Texas built an AI that turns brain scans into sentences. But it only worked after learning each person's brain for about sixteen hours. And a decoder trained on one brain... was useless on anyone else. Every brain speaks its own language. So the people Max knows best are the only ones he can really read. [tense] Which means whoever wrote that note... knows him very, very well. And even then, people don't think in neat sentences. Scientists who sampled random moments of people's thoughts found actual words only about a quarter of the time. [deadpan] The rest is pictures, feelings, and a lot of people thinking about absolutely nothing. [tense] Two p.m. The office. And there's a woman who has been watching Max. All. Day. Max reads her. And gets... nothing. Not static. Not music. Total silence. [tense] No thoughts at all. Either she's a robot... or she's hiding them on purpose. Which is exactly what a mind reader would do. [pause] She isn't hiding anything. She's one of the people who don't have an inner voice at all. This is real. Researchers only gave it a name in 2024: anendophasia. Some people live their whole lives without that little voice in their head. Many of them never knew everyone else had one. [playful] Quick question. Is there a voice in your head reading this to you right now? Tell us in the comments. [deadpan] Oh, and she was staring because Max had toothpaste on his face. Since breakfast. Suspect four, cleared.

[tense] Suspect two. Dave. Best friend. Knows everything about Max. Max reads him. And hears... [deadpan] "Baa baa black sheep, have you any wool..." Max reads harder. "Yes sir, yes sir, three bags full." [tense] Dave is blocking him. On purpose. Which is exactly what a mind reader would do. [curious] And here's the thing, this is real too. In that same Texas study, people could beat the decoder just by thinking about something else on purpose. Counting. Naming animals. [playful] So if a mind reader ever comes for you, start counting by sevens. You're welcome. And if that just saved your secrets, smash like. [sarcastic] And Max, if you're listening, please stay out of MY head. It's private in there. [pause] ...It's not about Dave. Max spends nine hours outside Dave's house. Dave sings "Baa Baa Black Sheep" for all nine. [tense] Then Dave cracks. One tiny thought slips through. [whisper] "...please don't let him find out about the ducks." [deadpan] Dave is not a mind reader. Dave is just terrified of ducks. Suspect two, cleared.

[tense] Nine p.m. Max goes to the big match to clear his head. Bad idea. Sixty thousand people. Your brain is brilliant at picking out one voice in a noisy room and ignoring the rest. It's called the cocktail party effect. [tense] But thoughts don't come through your ears. There's nothing to filter. [building] Kick-off. Sixty thousand minds switch on. "Goal!" "Hungry." "Did I leave the oven on?" "Why is that man screaming?" [sarcastic] Even the team mascot is thinking about quitting. [urgent] Eleven fifty-eight. Two minutes to midnight. One suspect left.

[quiet] Max gets home. The kitchen light is on. Mum is waiting. She knows when he's lying. She knows when he's sad. She always has. [tense] Max takes a breath. And reads his mum's mind properly, for the first time in his life. [warm] And he doesn't find a mind reader. He finds... himself. Every birthday. Every scraped knee. The first time he said "Mum." [quiet] And here's something real about memory. Every time you remember something, your brain rebuilds it. A little different each time. [warm] So Mum doesn't remember Max exactly as he was. She remembers him a little better. Every single time. [pause] Mum didn't write the note. Mum doesn't need superpowers. She's been reading him his whole life. [tense] Then... the clock strikes midnight.

[whisper] Something scratches at the back door. [tense] It walks in. Sits down. And stares straight into Max's soul. [pause] It was the dog. [sarcastic] How did a dog write a note? We're not answering that. [curious] But a dog reading minds? That part's real. Dogs can tell a happy human face from an angry one. They follow where we look and where we point. Their brains even react to the emotion in our voices. Sir Biscuit has been reading Max for years. Every mood. Every lie. Every time he was sad. [laughing] And what was he thinking the whole time? The answer was the very first thought Max ever read. [deadpan] "FOOD."
[warm] Max learned two things today. The people who love you don't need to read your mind. They already know you. And never, ever let a dog know your secrets.
[playful] Whose mind would you read first? And whose would you never, ever read? Comments. [sarcastic] And Max, I'm still not telling you about the duck.
